source.title: Distillation Scaling Laws
source.authors: Dan Busbridge; Amitis Shidani; Floris Weers; Jason Ramapuram; Etai Littwin; Russ Webb

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures language-model validation cross-entropy across model sizes, token budgets, and compute budgets, and fits scaling laws using supervised language-model runs. It also extends the analysis to distillation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own supervised and distillation scaling-law fits, extrapolation results, compute-optimal allocations, and downstream evaluations. Cited results from other studies are not extracted as rows. Architecture and hyperparameter settings are not outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own supervised law L(N,D) to 73 C4 runs using fixed-model and IsoFLOP protocols, as in Hoffmann et al. It reports fit error, extrapolation, compute-optimal exponents and downstream evaluations. It then extends the same power-law form to distillation pretraining. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors propose a distillation scaling law: student loss is a power law in student size and distillation tokens, modulated by teacher loss through a broken power law that captures the capacity gap. Distillation beats supervised learning only below a student-size-dependent compute or token threshold, and only when the teacher already exists or is reused. Given enough compute or data, supervised learning matches or beats distillation, and it is preferable when a teacher must be trained for a single student.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses controlled transformer language-model scaling experiments and validation cross-entropy, with µP, English-only C4, non-embedding parameter counts, and untied fit coefficients. It also introduces a distillation-specific law rather than only reproducing the supervised scaling setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper states that fitted coefficients depend on architecture and dataset choices and that parameter/FLOP counting affects fitted exponents. Its distillation results also show a capacity gap depending on teacher capability.
record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The study uses the English-only C4 dataset and transformer architectures only. The authors say the fitted distillation coefficients are specific to their architecture and dataset, and note that larger-token runs repeat data. Their downstream reasoning evaluations are near-random for most models.
record.rows_left_out: No per-task numerical downstream scores were transcribed from Figure 35 because the text does not state those values; the reported aggregate relationship and the explicit GSM8K/MMLU qualification are recorded in r6–r7. Other figure-only loss points are not listed individually because the paper reports aggregate fits and textual summaries.

untested.parts: Other datasets, architectures, and scales beyond 12.6B parameters and 512B tokens; a law in compute alone.
Predicting runs orders of magnitude larger than the fit set. Extrapolation here stays inside the 143M–12.6B range.
Whether Kaplan-style versus Hoffmann-style accounting changes the split in this data. Stability of the exponents across data or schedules.
All of it. Aspect ratio is fixed (dmodel/nlayers = 128) and shape is not varied.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer. Repeated data: it occurs in the larger runs, but its effect is not measured.
Reasoning-heavy tasks with non-trivial scores. Predicting downstream scores from small runs.
Curves bending away from a single power law in supervised training. Comparison of fitting methods or schedules.

missing.what: Relative error of the 2N FLOP approximation versus full counting: −39.74% at 103M down to −7.42% at 12.6B; the paper's corrected approximation errs below 0.4%.
Distillation compute-optimal analogues a′ = 0.664 and b′ = 0.335, showing a student-size-heavy split under a fixed teacher, unlike the supervised near-equal split.
Supervised irreducible loss E = 1.220, lower than Hoffmann et al.; the authors suspect this is due to µP, a setup dependence of the fitted law.
Statement that tied coefficients (Hoffmann γ = 1, Kaplan β = 1) fit and extrapolate significantly worse than untied ones.

record.verdict_notes: The study's main contribution is distillation; the supervised fit serves as its baseline but is a genuine Chinchilla-style replication (T1). V2 support is limited to modest within-range extrapolation. The 'primary driver of differing exponents' claim in r8 comes from Porian et al. and should not be credited as the study's own finding. The repeated-data limitation relies on a cited result (Muennighoff et al.) and is not tested.

versions.untested_parts: The reported supervised scaling fit is for the paper's English C4 and fixed-aspect-ratio transformer setup; it does not establish the law for all language-model setups.
Extrapolation is reported for weaker-to-stronger models within the paper's experimental setup, not for arbitrary architectures or datasets.
The compute-optimal exponents are reported for this supervised setup; other model families, data, and fit/counting choices are not comprehensively compared.
The study does not sweep depth, width, or architecture shape while holding parameter count fixed.

It studies distillation pretraining, but not other modalities, fine-tuning, transfer, or a systematic repeated-data comparison. The authors state that their coefficients are specific to their architecture and dataset choices.
Downstream evaluations are limited to the reported English tasks and C4-trained models; the authors note the dataset is not well suited to probing reasoning.
The paper argues that parameter-counting and setup choices affect fitted laws, but does not systematically compare fitting methods or show supervised curves bending away from a single power law.

rows.subject: Supervised language-model runs (aggregate fit; 73 samples)
rows.size_stated: Models range from 143M to 12.6B parameters; parameters in the scaling law are non-embedding parameters.
rows.operation_detail: Fit supervised validation cross-entropy as a function of model parameters and training tokens.
rows.measure: Validation cross-entropy as a function of parameter count and training tokens
rows.value: The fitted form is L(N,D)=E+(A/N^α+B/D^β)^γ; estimates: A=3355, B=18186, E=1.220, α=0.408, β=0.431, γ=0.452. The paper reports ≲1% relative prediction error for the supervised fit.
rows.uncertainty: 90% bootstrap confidence intervals are reported for the coefficients in Table 6 (4096 resamples).
rows.note: The paper reports a fitted aggregate law rather than separate loss values for every run. The fit combines fixed-model/varied-data runs and IsoFLOP profiles.
rows.check: Value is correct. Appendix E.2 counts 74 runs, while the fit (F.1) uses 73 samples. Range is 143M–12.6B non-embedding parameters, about two orders of magnitude.

source_check.locator_found: Equation 1; Appendix E.2; Appendix F.1; Table 6

rows.subject: Supervised language-model runs (aggregate fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit on weaker models and compare predictions with stronger-model observations.
rows.measure: Relative prediction error for validation cross-entropy
rows.value: The supervised scaling law has ≲1% relative prediction error, including when extrapolated from weaker to stronger models.
rows.note: The paper describes the extrapolation result in text; it does not give a separate numerical error specifically for the extrapolated subset.
rows.check: Condition should state the setup. The extrapolation fit uses L ≥ 2.2 runs (48 of 73 samples) to predict lower-loss runs inside the same 143M–12.6B range. That span is not orders of magnitude larger. No extrapolation-only error is given; Figure 5a shows errors within about ±1%.

rows.subject: Distilled student language models (aggregate fit; 697 samples)
rows.size_stated: Students range from 143M to 12.6B parameters; teachers range from 198M to 7.75B in the main experimental protocols.
rows.operation_detail: Fit student validation cross-entropy using student parameters, distillation tokens, and teacher cross-entropy.

conditions.value: English-only C4; teacher and student trained on different splits

rows.measure: Student validation cross-entropy as a function of student size, distillation tokens, and teacher cross-entropy
rows.value: The proposed law uses power-law terms in student size and distillation tokens, with a broken-power-law transition in teacher cross-entropy. Fitted estimates include α′=0.321, β′=0.637, γ′=0.764, c0=2.549, c1=522.6, f1=0.090, and d1=1.315. The paper reports ≲1% relative prediction error for the fit.
rows.uncertainty: 90% bootstrap confidence intervals are reported for the fitted coefficients in Table 6 (4096 resamples).
rows.note: This is evidence for scaling behavior in distillation, but the proposed law is not simply the supervised law: it includes teacher cross-entropy and a transition associated with the capacity gap.
rows.check: Remove V7. The row reports the distillation law's form and coefficients, not sensitivity to fitting choices. Student loss keeps a power law in NS and DS (same inner term as Eq. 1), multiplied by a teacher-dependent broken power law. The capacity-gap qualification belongs in the label, not the state.

source_check.correct: For V5, state=partial: Equation 8 retains parameter/token power-law components but adds teacher cross-entropy and a broken factor depending on teacher loss relative to the student's supervised-equivalent loss.

rows.uncertainty: 90% bootstrap intervals are shown in Table 6 as (0.513, 0.513) for a and (0.486, 0.486) for b.

rows.subject: Supervised language-model scaling fits (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Assess parameter and FLOP counting choices and their effect on scaling-law fits.

conditions.value: non-embedding parameters used in the scaling law
includes context-dependent attention and vocabulary terms

rows.measure: Sensitivity of fitted scaling behavior to parameter and compute accounting
rows.baseline: Common parameter/FLOP counting approaches discussed in the paper
rows.value: The authors state that non-embedding parameters give the cleanest fit and extrapolation, and that embedding and attention FLOP accounting can produce systematic errors; they identify these accounting differences as primary drivers of differing reported exponents.
rows.note: This supports setup-dependence of fitted laws. The paper does not provide a controlled table of alternative fits under each counting convention.
rows.check: The claim that counting choices are the 'primary drivers' of differing exponents is cited from Porian et al. (footnote 8); it is not the study's own result. The study's own evidence is twofold: untied coefficients give 'significantly better fit and extrapolation' (footnote 1, no numbers), and Table 13 shows the 2N FLOP approximation errs by −39.7% at 103M and −7.4% at 12.6B. No alternative-fit exponents are reported.
